cls: Thyroid hormone analogue used as a lipid-lowering agent (D-isomer of thyroxine)
pharm: The dextrorotatory isomer of thyroxine that lowers serum cholesterol by increasing hepatic LDL catabolism, but with residual thyromimetic cardiac stimulation
quick: Historically started 1-2 mg/day, increased to ~4-8 mg/day (no longer marketed)
Was taken orally; food relevance limited

summary: Dextrothyroxine (sodium dextrothyroxine, D-thyroxine) is the dextrorotatory isomer of the thyroid hormone thyroxine and was formerly used as a lipid-lowering agent to reduce serum cholesterol. It lowers cholesterol by increasing hepatic catabolism and excretion of low-density lipoprotein. However, it was found to have significant thyromimetic cardiac effects (tachycardia, arrhythmia, angina) and was associated with increased cardiac events in the Coronary Drug Project, leading to its WITHDRAWAL from the US market. It is therefore not a current FDA-approved therapy; this record is provided for historical and reference purposes only and is compiled from older pharmacology literature rather than a current label. Historical dosing started low (1-2 mg/day) and was titrated upward, but it should not be used as a lipid-lowering agent in modern practice given safer alternatives (statins) and its cardiac hazards.
indications: Historical: adjunct to reduce elevated serum cholesterol in euthyroid patients (no longer recommended; withdrawn)
Historical/limited: occasionally cited for hypothyroidism, but L-thyroxine is the standard agent

moa: Dextrothyroxine is the D-isomer of thyroxine. It lowers serum cholesterol mainly by stimulating hepatic LDL-receptor activity and the catabolism and biliary excretion of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, an action of thyroid hormones on lipid metabolism. Although the D-isomer was intended to retain the lipid effect with less metabolic/cardiac stimulation than L-thyroxine, in practice it still exerts thyromimetic actions on the heart (positive chronotropic and inotropic effects, increased myocardial oxygen demand), which underlies its cardiac toxicity and contributed to its withdrawal.

absolute: Known cardiovascular disease - angina, arrhythmia, heart failure, recent myocardial infarction
relative: Concurrent use of other cardiac stimulants or anticoagulants

preg: Dextrothyroxine is not recommended in pregnancy. As a withdrawn agent with thyromimetic cardiac effects and no current role, it should be avoided; standard care for lipids in pregnancy does not include this drug.
lact: Avoid during breastfeeding. Thyroid-hormone analogues can be excreted in milk, and the drug has no current therapeutic role.
renal: Limited data; use with caution if it were ever considered. No modern dosing guidance exists as the drug is withdrawn.
hepatic: Use with caution; the cholesterol-lowering action depends on hepatic LDL catabolism and hepatic dysfunction may alter response. No current dosing recommendations exist.

major: Oral anticoagulants (warfarin) - thyroid hormones potentiate anticoagulant effect; risk of bleeding
Cardiac stimulants and sympathomimetics - additive cardiac stimulation/arrhythmia
Catecholamines/adrenaline - increased risk of coronary insufficiency
moderate: Antidiabetic agents - thyromimetic effect may increase requirements
Digitalis glycosides - altered response and arrhythmia risk
Other thyroid preparations - additive thyromimetic effect
minor: Cholestyramine and bile-acid sequestrants - reduce absorption
interactions.diagnostics: Alters thyroid-function test results and lipid panels; may affect coagulation tests via warfarin interaction

serious: Increased cardiovascular events/mortality (Coronary Drug Project finding)

monitoring: ECG and cardiac symptoms during any use
counsel: This medicine is no longer used for lowering cholesterol because safer options exist and it can strain the heart
If you have any heart condition you should not take it
Report palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness or a racing heart immediately
Do not start or stop other heart or blood-thinning medicines without advice
Modern cholesterol treatment uses statins and other proven, safer agents
Discuss any historical prescription of this drug with your doctor
pk: Lipid effect develops over weeks; cardiac thyromimetic effects sooner
Long, in keeping with thyroid hormone analogues (days)

Historical product - store per manufacturer, protect from light
pearls: WITHDRAWN in the US and NOT FDA-approved for current use - this record is historical/reference only
D-isomer of thyroxine once used to lower cholesterol by increasing hepatic LDL catabolism
Abandoned because of thyromimetic cardiac toxicity and excess cardiovascular events (Coronary Drug Project)
Contraindicated in cardiac disease, arrhythmia and recent myocardial infarction
Potentiates warfarin and additive with cardiac stimulants
Modern lipid management uses statins/ezetimibe/PCSK9 inhibitors, not dextrothyroxine
missed: This is a withdrawn medicine not in current use, so missed-dose guidance is not applicable. Any patient with a historical prescription should consult their doctor about appropriate modern alternatives.
overdose: Overdose produces thyrotoxicosis-like effects: tachycardia, arrhythmia, angina, tremor, agitation and hyperthermia, potentially precipitating a thyroid-storm-like state. Management is supportive: discontinue the drug, control heart rate with beta-blockade, treat arrhythmia and hyperthermia, and provide supportive care; effects may be prolonged because of the long half-life.
